transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I came in because I feel like I can’t stop starting things. Like projects, plans, systems—one after another. At work I’ll make these huge plans, reorganize timelines, map out new initiatives, and then I’ll also start building certification schedules for myself like I’m going to completely upgrade my whole career in two months.

And then at home it’s the same thing. I’ll decide the home network needs to be redone, or I’ll start planning upgrades, or I’ll message old contacts because suddenly it feels really important to reconnect or pitch ideas or get something moving. It’s not just being productive, exactly. It gets intense, like I blow past what would normally be reasonable, and I don’t really stop on my own.

Usually it takes my wife saying, “You need to slow down,” or my director at work stepping in and kind of putting limits around what I’m doing. That’s the part that made me think I should come in, because it’s starting to feel like I’m not steering it as much as I should be.
When you get into these intense stretches, do you need less sleep than usual and still feel rested?

Yeah. That’s actually one of the things that makes it feel different from just being busy or stressed.

There have been these stretches where I’ll sleep, I don’t know, maybe three hours total, and then I’m just awake at like 3 or 4 in the morning. But it doesn’t feel like insomnia in the usual way, where I’m lying there miserable and exhausted. It’s more like I wake up sharp, like my brain is already on and lined up, and I’m thinking, “Great, I’ve got extra time now.” Like I’ve been handed bonus hours to get ahead.

And in the moment I don’t feel tired. I’ll get up and start planning things or looking at work stuff or making lists, and it feels almost efficient, like I’m being smart with the time. It’s usually only later, when someone points out that I’ve barely slept for a few nights, that I realize it might not be normal.
During these intense stretches, do you actually feel unusually upbeat or euphoric?

Yeah… I think so. Not always “happy” exactly, but there are definitely weeks where I feel almost electric, like everything is clicking and I’m unstoppable. It’s like I’ve got this charge running through me, and ideas feel brighter, faster, more obvious than they usually do.

At first it can feel really good, honestly. Like I’m finally operating at the level I’m supposed to be operating at. I’ll think, “This is me being capable, this is me finally not wasting time.” So yes, there’s an upbeat part to it, but it’s not just cheerful. It’s more intense than that.

And then it can flip really fast. Like if there’s a tiny delay, or my wife asks a normal question like, “Do you really need to do that right now?”—I can suddenly feel this surge of irritation, like she’s trying to slow me down on purpose. Or if someone at work questions the timing of something, I’ll feel like they’re blocking momentum, even if they’re probably just asking a reasonable question.

So it’s kind of both. I can feel amazing and driven, like nothing can stop me, but also really impatient and snappy if anyone gets in the way.
During these energized stretches, do you also feel depressed or down?

Yeah… yes. I mean, it’s not always separate from the energized stuff in a clean way, if that makes sense. There are definitely stretches where I wake up and it’s like the opposite of that charged, unstoppable feeling. I’ll open my eyes and immediately feel like some failed version of myself, like I’ve already disappointed everyone before the day has even started.

It’s heavy. Not dramatic exactly, just… flat. Like everything in me is weighted down. And even normal things feel weirdly hard. My wife can ask something completely reasonable, like what time I’m leaving or whether I remembered something, and it feels like too much to answer. Not because she’s doing anything wrong — she’s not — but because forming the response feels like effort I don’t have.

And then I feel guilty because I know she’s just asking a normal question, and I’m sitting there feeling like I can’t even be a normal husband in that moment. It’s embarrassing to say out loud, but yes, I do get down like that.
During those high-energy periods, have you ever heard or seen things that other people said weren’t there, or believed something others thought was clearly untrue?

Yeah… that’s harder to talk about, but yes. During the really driven stretches — the ones where I’m barely sleeping and I’m convinced I’m pushing these big plans forward — I’ve had things happen that, looking back, don’t seem normal.

One thing is the server noise. At work, there’s that constant hum and clicking and fans spinning, and when I’m in that state, especially when I’m running on almost no sleep, it can start to sound like comments. Not like a clear person standing next to me having a conversation, exactly, but like little remarks inside the noise. Like I’ll hear something that feels directed at me, or like it’s reacting to what I’m doing. In the moment it feels meaningful, like I’m picking up on something I’m supposed to notice.

And with messages at work, I’ve definitely read hidden threats into them. Like someone sends a normal email or Teams message about a deadline or a system change, and I’ll suddenly feel like there’s a warning underneath it, like they’re signaling that I’m being watched or that they’re trying to box me in. At the time it feels obvious, like I’ve cracked the subtext and everyone else is either missing it or pretending not to see it.

Then later, when I’m calmer, I can look at the same message and think, “That was just a normal work message.” But when I’m in it, it doesn’t feel like a maybe. It feels real.
Have you ever had those experiences—like hearing comments in the server noise or feeling messages had hidden threats—at a time when you were not in one of those high-energy or depressed periods?

Yeah… yes, that’s happened too. And honestly that’s one of the parts that makes it harder for me to explain away as just “I was too keyed up” or “I was really low,” because there have been stretches where I wasn’t obviously in either place.

Like, I can think of a few times that lasted a few weeks where I was more… calm isn’t exactly the word, maybe flat. I was going to work, coming home, not feeling especially energized or like I had some huge mission, but also not crushed in the way I get when I’m really depressed. Just kind of neutral, or dulled out.

And even then, I’d still look at Teams statuses and feel like they meant something coded. Like someone changing from available to away, or putting up a certain kind of status message, would feel like a warning aimed at me. Not just “oh, maybe they’re busy,” but like there was a signal in it, like I was supposed to understand that people were watching what I was doing or that something was about to happen.

And the hearing-comments thing has happened then too, though more briefly. Like not a long conversation, not constant, but I’d be alone and hear a short comment, almost like someone had said something from nearby, and then I’d check and no one was there. Or I’d realize it didn’t really make sense where it came from. It’s unsettling because I can’t always attach it to being sleep-deprived or worked up.

So… yes. There have been times when I wasn’t in one of those intense high or low periods, and it still happened.
Was there ever a time when those unusual experiences lasted for two weeks or more while you were not feeling high, energized, depressed, or unusually irritable?

Yes. Yeah, there have been times like that. Not just a day or two where I could blame it on being tired or stressed, but stretches that went on for a few weeks.

I wasn’t feeling especially up during those times. I wasn’t in that mode where I’m talking fast or feeling like I’ve figured everything out, and I wasn’t really depressed in the heavy way either. More like… flat. Going through the routine. Work, home, work, home. Kind of dulled out, but not in a big dramatic mood state.

And even then, the Teams stuff still happened. I’d see someone’s status change, or see a short status message, and it would feel like it meant something more than it said. Like it was coded somehow, like a warning directed at me. I know that sounds strange when I say it now, because it’s just a status icon or a sentence, but at the time it didn’t feel random. It felt like there was a message underneath it that I was supposed to catch.

And I still had the brief comments too. Not constant, not like an ongoing conversation, but I’d hear something short when nobody was there. Like a quick remark, enough that I’d look around or stop what I was doing. And this was during those flatter, calmer stretches, not when I was especially energized or really down.

So yes, there have been several times like that, including periods that lasted a few weeks.
